top.line: Yes or no is a decision's least interesting part
top.para: Humans or agents in the loop are mostly asked for a yes or no. Agency needs options, context, depth, time, incentives, escalation and authority, scored on a seven-level scale capped by the weakest dimension. Below level 3 the decider holds liability; above it, review becomes QA, and proven drafts become rules.

s0.line: Agency has seven dimensions, and the weakest caps it
s0.para: A yes or no is not agency. Seven observable dimensions set the level, and below level 3 accountability belongs to whoever designed the decision point and their chain. Above it, review is QA that fixes the source, and at the top proven cases become rules under a behaviour policy, for agents as for people.

s1.line: If only yes is realistic, there is no agency
s1.para: I review agent-prepared emails daily, and no agent sends on its own except one security email. The go or no-go is the dull part, and a no leaves someone with a problem, so yes is tempting. A prompt asking to add label 756-459-3214 gave no way to know what was being authorised.

s2.line: Whatever you punish, you teach the opposite answer
s2.para: Punish wrong yeses and people say no; punish delay and they say yes. Ritov and Baron called the tendency to judge acts more harshly than omissions omission bias in 1990. Agency needs symmetric incentives with room for honest error, time to decide and somewhere to escalate, or mistakes are predictable and unfair to blame.

s3.line: Everything a decider sees is a compression of reality
s3.para: A summary, description or draft is fine until there is a question, and then the decider must expand it to the data, steps and decisions behind it. Provenance and zoomable fractal semantic graphs make that possible. Without an answer to why, there is no explainability and the decision is a guess.

s4.line: Accountability without agency is just liability
s4.para: Drivers supervising automation took between 1.9 and 25.7 seconds to take back control, and Bainbridge's 1983 Ironies of Automation warned of this. The moral crumple zone and the Post Office sub-postmasters show who gets blamed. When the person in the loop lacks agency, responsibility should sit with whoever designed the decision point and up their chain.

s5.line: Seven levels run from rubber stamp to delegator
s5.para: Seven dimensions each cap the level, and the lowest cap wins. Levels run from 0, rubber stamp, through informed yes or no, looking behind, resourced, editor and owner of the source, to 6, delegator. Of fourteen cases, eight sit at level 0; a senior clinician is at 4, my draft review at 5.

s6.line: Agents are deciders too, and rules should decide
s6.para: An agent asked whether a draft is fine with no tools, budget or escalation is a rubber stamp, while the Hope or enforcement controller reaches level 3. Agents should meet the same standard as people. The final decision should be code, a decision tree of checks: models propose, rules decide, people own the rules.

s7.line: Review is QA that fixes the source, not output
s7.para: Reviewing a draft means asking how we got here: often the CRM record is missing something, so the fix goes to the record or the objectives. Each such fix validates many earlier decisions. Ownership drives engagement, and the workflow uses labels and recipient-less drafts as a small interface with the agents.

s8.line: Drafts that keep passing unchanged become automated rules
s8.para: When one kind of draft keeps coming back correct, the behaviour policy changes to let that agent send that kind of email and nothing else. Proven cases shrink what needs expert review and allow cheaper models, such as Sonnet and Haiku 5.5. The most senior person should review only what is genuinely new.

s9.line: EU law already sets a floor at level 3
s9.para: Article 14(4) requires overseers to understand a system's limits, resist over-reliance and be able to override or stop it; Article 26(2) requires competence, training, authority and support. Below level 3 oversight is on paper only. The problem is old judgement; automating flows without explainability makes it bigger.

s10.line: Find each decision point's weakest dimension and fix it
s10.para: List decision points, run the assessment and fix the weakest dimension first. Replace identifiers with things, make why answerable, match incentives, move accountability below level 3, treat review as QA and turn proven cases into rules. Drafted from two voice memos by Dinis Cruz on 8 October 2026.
